title: Differences of enumerable sets

based_on.title: How to approximate fuzzy sets: mind-changes and the Ershov Hierarchy
based_on.pages: Article 55; section The Classical Ershov Hierarchy, Definition 3, Remark 1 and the two-change case of Theorem 3

summary: Removing one enumerable set from another is exactly what a computable binary approximation can describe with at most two revisions per input, starting from zero.
abstract: A list can supply evidence that a number belongs to a set, while a second list can later cancel that evidence. The numbers that enter the first list and never enter the second form a difference of enumerable sets. Their membership guesses start at zero, can rise to one, and can return to zero at most once. Conversely, every computable approximation with this two-revision bound can be reconstructed from two enumerable lists. This describes a class containing both recognizable sets and sets whose exclusion is recognizable, as well as examples of neither kind. The bound counts revisions, not the waiting time before the last revision, so even one permitted revision does not provide a decision procedure.
